overview.title: Fine-tuning RoBERTa on IMDb, and the opening of 'What makes the Transformer effective?'
overview.main_topic: Adding a classification head on top of the pretrained RoBERTa backbone (first-token pooling, dropout, a 768-unit ReLU layer, a sigmoid output), fine-tuning it with Adam at 5e-5 for one epoch to reach about 93.7% test accuracy on IMDb, then starting section 15.5 with the story of Word2Vec
overview.central_idea: A pretrained Transformer encoder becomes a strong sentiment classifier with only a tiny head and a single epoch of low-learning-rate fine-tuning: it beats the 90% ceiling of chapter 14's bigram model. The page then turns to why Transformers work so well, starting from Word2Vec's idea of turning word co-occurrence into vector proximity.
overview.importance: This closes the practical arc of the chapter (pretrain once, fine-tune cheaply) and gives the concrete payoff of transfer learning for text: about 94% on IMDb versus 90% for the best model trained from scratch in chapter 14 (p.428). It also opens the conceptual section 15.5, whose Word2Vec comparison (pp.486-488) explains attention as embedding-space refinement.

summary:
The page finishes section 15.4.4 and starts section 15.5.

**Listing 15.22** turns the pretrained RoBERTa **backbone** (loaded on p.480) into a binary classifier. It reuses the backbone's own input tensors (`backbone.input`), runs them through the backbone to get one 768-dimensional hidden vector per token, and keeps only the vector of the **first token** (`x[:, 0, :]`, the callout: "Uses the hidden representation of the first token"). On top it stacks `Dropout(0.1)` → `Dense(768, relu)` → `Dropout(0.1)` → `Dense(1, sigmoid)`, and wraps everything in a functional `keras.Model`.

**Listing 15.23** compiles the model with **Adam at a learning rate of 5e-5**, `binary_crossentropy` loss and accuracy, and calls `fit()` on the preprocessed training set with the validation set. No `epochs` argument is passed, so Keras trains for its default of **one epoch**. Every weight, including the roughly 125 million of the backbone (figure not in the book), is updated: this is full fine-tuning.

Evaluating on the test set returns `[0.168127179145813, 0.9366399645805359]`: a loss of about 0.168 and **93.7% accuracy**. The authors stress that this comes after **a single epoch** and beats the **90% ceiling** of chapter 14 (the bigram model, p.428). The model is far more expensive to run than that bigram classifier, but the benefit is clear, and this is only the *base* RoBERTa; the larger (~300M-parameter) model reaches **over 95%**.

**Section 15.5, "What makes the Transformer effective?"** opens with history. In 2013 Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google built **Word2Vec**, a pretrained embedding similar to the chapter 14 CBOW model. Its objective turned **correlation relationships between words into distance relationships**: each word gets a vector, and vectors are optimized so that frequently co-occurring words have a dot-product (cosine proximity) near 1. The sentence, and the "word arithmetic" discovery, continue on p.486.

paragraphs.excerpt: In just a single epoch of training, our model reached 93%, a
paragraphs.what_it_says: After one epoch the fine-tuned model reaches 93% test accuracy (93.66% in the printout), better than the 90% ceiling of chapter 14. It is much more expensive than the bigram classifier, but the benefits are clear, and it is only the small RoBERTa; the larger 300-million-parameter model would exceed 95%.
paragraphs.what_it_means:
Pretraining on about 160 GB of web text (p.479) has already taught the backbone a rich representation of English: syntax, negation, sentiment-bearing phrases. Fine-tuning only has to point that representation at the sentiment label, which is why one pass over 20,000 reviews is enough. The models of chapter 14 had to learn everything from IMDb alone, and their embeddings overfitted before they were good (p.437).

The trade-off is cost. The bigram model was a single linear layer over a 30,000-dimensional multi-hot vector (about 30,000 parameters). RoBERTa base has on the order of 125 million parameters and runs a dozen attention layers over every token (numbers not in the book), so each prediction costs several orders of magnitude more compute.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the concrete payoff of the pretrain-then-fine-tune paradigm the chapter has been building towards, and the reason pretrained Transformers displaced task-specific models across NLP. It also previews the scaling argument of chapter 16: bigger pretrained models (base to large) buy more accuracy.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: '93%' rounds 93.66% down; 'just a single epoch' follows from `fit()` having no `epochs` argument (Keras defaults to 1). Fine-tuned RoBERTa-large is reported around 95-96% on IMDb in the literature, consistent with the authors' 'over 95%'. The published RoBERTa-large has about 355 million parameters, so '300 million' is a round figure.

paragraphs.excerpt: In 2013, at Google, Tomas Mikolov and his colleagues noticed something remarkable.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 15.5 opens in 2013. Mikolov's team at Google built the pretrained embedding Word2Vec, similar to the chapter 14 CBOW embedding. Like CBOW, its objective turned correlation between words into distance in an embedding space: one vector per vocabulary word, optimized so that the dot-product (cosine proximity) of vectors for frequently co-occurring words would be close to 1 (the sentence finishes on p.486, where rarely co-occurring words go toward 0).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The authors start their explanation of the Transformer's effectiveness with a much simpler model on purpose. Word2Vec makes the core principle easy to see: statistics of which words appear together are converted into geometry, so that words used in similar contexts end up pointing in similar directions.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The rest of the section (pp.486-488) argues that a Transformer follows the same principle, with attention as the mechanism that keeps pulling co-occurring tokens closer, layer after layer. Understanding Word2Vec's objective is the foundation of that argument.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) comes in two variants, CBOW (predict a word from its surrounding words) and skip-gram (predict surrounding words from a word). With negative sampling, the probability that a pair co-occurs is modeled as $\sigma(\mathbf{u}_w \cdot \mathbf{v}_c)$ and pushed toward 1 for observed pairs and toward 0 for random pairs. Cosine proximity is the dot-product of the length-normalized vectors, $\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert}$.

terminology.meaning: A 2013 family of shallow models from Google that learn word vectors from co-occurrence in a context window.
An embedding objective that predicts a word from the average of its neighbours' embeddings; built in chapter 14.
Similarity of two vectors measured by the cosine of the angle between them: 1 for the same direction, 0 for orthogonal.

p.486: the sentence continues and introduces 'word arithmetic' and attention as embedding refinement

concepts.name: Fine-tuning a pretrained Transformer
concepts.definition: Taking a model pretrained on a large unlabeled corpus, attaching a small task-specific head, and continuing training on labeled task data with a small learning rate.
concepts.intuition: The backbone already 'reads' English well. Fine-tuning teaches it what to look for in this task, without starting from scratch.
concepts.technical: In Listing 15.23 all weights are trainable (the backbone is not frozen), and the learning rate is 5e-5, about 20 times smaller than Adam's default of 1e-3, so the pretrained weights move only slightly. One epoch is enough to reach 93.7% on IMDb.
concepts.significance: It turns the expensive pretraining (a day on 1,024 GPUs, p.480) into a reusable asset: each new task costs only a short training run.
concepts.example: RoBERTa base + Dropout/Dense/Dropout/Dense head, trained for one epoch on 20,000 IMDb reviews → 93.66% test accuracy.
concepts.misconception: Fine-tuning does not mean only the new head is trained. Here the whole network is updated; freezing the backbone would be 'feature extraction'.

concepts.name: First-token pooling
concepts.definition: Using the encoder's output vector at position 0 (RoBERTa's `<s>` start token, BERT's `[CLS]`) as a fixed-size representation of the whole sequence.
concepts.intuition: Because attention is bidirectional, the first token can attend to every other token in every layer, so its final vector can gather information about the whole review.
concepts.technical: The backbone outputs a tensor of shape `(batch, sequence_length, 768)`; `x[:, 0, :]` slices out shape `(batch, 768)`. The start token sits at position 0 because the `StartEndPacker` (p.483) prepends it to every sequence.
concepts.significance: It reproduces the head used when BERT/RoBERTa were evaluated on classification tasks, so the model's representations are used the way they were designed.
concepts.example: For a 512-token review, 512 × 768 numbers come out of the backbone; only the first 768 are passed to the classifier.
concepts.misconception: The first token is not special in itself before training; it is useful because the stack of bidirectional attention layers lets it summarize the sequence, and fine-tuning makes it summarize what the task needs.

concepts.name: Transfer learning for text
concepts.definition: Reusing knowledge learned on one task or dataset (pretraining on web text) to improve performance on another (IMDb sentiment).
concepts.intuition: Like hiring an experienced reader and teaching them a narrow skill, instead of teaching someone to read from scratch.
concepts.technical: The pretrained token embeddings and attention weights act as a very good initialization, in the same spirit as reusing the CBOW embedding to prime the LSTM in chapter 14 (p.442), but for the entire network instead of one layer.
concepts.significance: It explains the jump from the 84-90% of chapter 14's from-scratch models to 93.7%, and it is the basis of the LLMs of chapter 16.
concepts.example: Chapter 14 LSTM: about 84% (p.437). Bigram: 90% (p.428). Fine-tuned RoBERTa base: 93.7%. RoBERTa large: over 95%.
concepts.misconception: The gain is not free: the larger model is far more expensive to run, as the authors point out.

concepts.name: Word2Vec
concepts.definition: A pretrained word embedding from Mikolov et al. (Google, 2013) whose training objective turns word co-occurrence into vector proximity.
concepts.intuition: Words that keep showing up together are pulled together in space; words that rarely do are pushed apart.
concepts.technical: One vector per vocabulary word; the dot-product (cosine proximity) of frequently co-occurring words is optimized toward 1, of rarely co-occurring words toward 0 (p.486).
concepts.significance: Section 15.5 uses it as the simple model that shows the same principle the Transformer relies on.
concepts.example: 'coffee' and 'cup' co-occur often, so their vectors end up with high cosine similarity.
concepts.misconception: Word2Vec is not a deep network: it is a shallow, single-layer model (p.487).

code.title: Extending the base RoBERTa model for classification
code.original_code:
inputs = backbone.input
x = backbone(inputs)
x = x[:, 0, :]
x = layers.Dropout(0.1)(x)
x = layers.Dense(768, activation="relu")(x)
x = layers.Dropout(0.1)(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(x)
classifier = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
code.what_it_does: Builds a functional Keras model that runs the pretrained RoBERTa backbone, takes the hidden vector of the first token, passes it through a small regularized MLP, and outputs the probability that a review is positive.

line_explanations.explanation: `backbone.input` reuses the backbone's own symbolic inputs. For a KerasHub backbone this is a dict with `token_ids` and `padding_mask`, exactly what the preprocessing of p.483 produces. Reusing them guarantees the new model accepts the same input format.
Calling the backbone on those inputs yields the last layer's hidden states, shape `(batch, sequence_length, 768)`: one contextual vector per token.

The callout: 'Uses the hidden representation of the first token'. Slicing position 0 on the sequence axis gives shape `(batch, 768)`, the vector of the start token, which can attend to the whole review.

Dropout 0.1, a 768-unit ReLU dense layer, dropout 0.1. This mirrors the classification head RoBERTa used (hidden size 768) and adds a little capacity and regularization. The dense layer has 768 × 768 + 768 = 590,592 parameters.
A single sigmoid unit outputs $p(\text{positive}\mid\text{review})$ in (0, 1), the standard binary-classification output (769 parameters).
Wraps inputs and outputs into a functional `keras.Model`. The backbone's weights are part of this model and remain trainable.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: dict of `token_ids` and `padding_mask`, each `(batch, sequence_length)`. Output: `(batch, 1)` probabilities.
code.algorithm: Encoder → first-token pooling → dropout → dense(relu) → dropout → dense(sigmoid).
code.theory_link: The bidirectional encoder (p.479) lets position 0 attend to all tokens, so its final vector can act as a sequence summary. Dropout regularizes the new head, which starts from random weights.

parameters.name: Dropout(0.1)
parameters.role: Randomly zeroes 10% of the features during training only; RoBERTa itself used 0.1 dropout.

parameters.name: Dense(768, relu)
parameters.role: Hidden layer of the head, the same width as RoBERTa base's hidden size.

pitfalls: Indexing `x[0]` instead of `x[:, 0, :]` would take the first *review* of the batch, not the first *token*.
If a different tokenizer or packing order were used, position 0 would not hold the start token the backbone was pretrained with.
The new head starts from random weights while the backbone is pretrained; a large learning rate could damage the backbone's weights early in training (hence 5e-5 in Listing 15.23).
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: check the shapes and the head's size
classifier.summary()
# or inspect the pooled tensor
print(backbone.output.shape)      # (None, None, 768)
print(x.shape)                    # (None, 1) at the end of the listing

code.title: Training the RoBERTa classification model
code.original_code:
classifier.compile(
    optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(5e-5),
    loss="binary_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
classifier.fit(
    preprocessed_train_ds,
    validation_data=preprocessed_val_ds,
)
code.what_it_does: Compiles the classifier with a small Adam learning rate and binary cross-entropy, then fine-tunes it for one epoch (the Keras default) on the preprocessed IMDb training set while reporting validation metrics.

line_explanations.explanation: `Adam(5e-5)`: a learning rate typical for fine-tuning BERT-style models (the BERT paper recommended 2e-5 to 5e-5). `binary_crossentropy` matches the single sigmoid output; `accuracy` is reported alongside.
`fit()` iterates over the tf.data dataset of `(inputs, label)` batches. No `epochs` argument → 1 epoch. Validation metrics are computed at the end of the epoch on `preprocessed_val_ds`.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: preprocessed batched datasets from p.483. Output: a `History` object; the model's weights (backbone and head) are updated in place.
code.algorithm: Mini-batch gradient descent with Adam over every trainable weight of backbone and head.
code.theory_link: A small learning rate keeps the pretrained representations largely intact while adapting them to the task; this is what distinguishes fine-tuning from training from scratch.

parameters.name: learning_rate = 5e-5
parameters.role: Step size; 20 × smaller than Adam's default 1e-3.

parameters.name: loss = binary_crossentropy
parameters.role: Negative log-likelihood of the correct label under the sigmoid output.

parameters.name: epochs (default 1)
parameters.role: Number of passes over the training data; one is enough here.

pitfalls: Using Adam's default 1e-3 often makes fine-tuning diverge or wipes out what the backbone learned during pretraining (catastrophic forgetting).
Fine-tuning a 125M-parameter model needs a GPU; on a CPU one epoch can take hours.
Running several epochs without monitoring validation loss can quickly overfit 20,000 reviews.

code.title: Evaluating the fine-tuned model on the test set
code.what_it_does: Computes the compiled loss and metrics over the whole preprocessed test set.

line_explanations.explanation: `evaluate()` runs inference over every test batch; no weights change.
Returns `[loss, accuracy]` in the order loss first, then metrics as listed in `compile()`: binary cross-entropy 0.168 and accuracy 93.66%.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: the preprocessed test dataset. Output: a list of two floats.
code.algorithm: Average of per-sample losses and fraction of correctly thresholded (0.5) predictions.
code.theory_link: Test performance measures generalization; it is the number comparable with chapter 14's results.
pitfalls: Results vary slightly between runs because of dropout, data shuffling and initialization of the head.

deeper.title: What does a test loss of 0.168 mean?
deeper.body:
Binary cross-entropy for one example is $-\log p_{\text{correct}}$, where $p_{\text{correct}}$ is the probability the model gives to the true label. An average loss of 0.168 means the *geometric mean* of $p_{\text{correct}}$ over the test set is $e^{-0.168} \approx 0.845$.

For comparison, a model that always says 0.5 has a loss of $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$. A confidently wrong prediction ($p_{\text{correct}} = 0.01$) costs $-\ln 0.01 \approx 4.6$ on its own, so a few confident mistakes among the 6.3% of errors account for much of the remaining loss. (Explanation not in the book.)

deeper.title: Where the 93.7% comes from: a scoreboard of IMDb models in the book
deeper.body:
- Bag-of-words (unigrams), linear model: about 88% (p.428)
- Bigrams, linear model: 90% (p.428), the 'ceiling' mentioned on this page
- LSTM with learned embedding: about 84% (p.437)
- Fine-tuned RoBERTa base, 1 epoch: 93.66% (this page)
- RoBERTa large: over 95% (this page, stated, not run)

The from-scratch sequence models of chapter 14 did *worse* than the bigram baseline because 20,000 reviews could not train good embeddings. Pretraining removes that bottleneck.

deeper.title: Analogy: hiring an experienced reader
deeper.body: Training the chapter 14 models is like teaching someone to read English using only 20,000 movie reviews, then asking for sentiment. Fine-tuning RoBERTa is like hiring someone who has read a large slice of the web and spending one afternoon showing them labeled reviews. The second person learns much faster, but they are also far more expensive to employ for every review you ask about.

misconceptions.correction: The backbone is not frozen, so all its weights are updated too; the small learning rate (5e-5) keeps those updates gentle.

misconceptions.claim: The model trained for many epochs to reach 93%.
misconceptions.correction: `fit()` is called without `epochs`, so it trains for Keras's default of one epoch, as the text stresses.

misconceptions.claim: A bigger pretrained model is always the better choice.
misconceptions.correction: The authors explicitly note the much higher cost of running RoBERTa compared with the bigram classifier; accuracy must be weighed against inference cost.
Word2Vec is a shallow embedding model from 2013 with no attention; section 15.5 compares it to Transformers because they share the co-occurrence-to-proximity principle, not the architecture.

takeaways: A pretrained encoder becomes a classifier by pooling one vector (the first token's) and adding a small dropout-regularized MLP with a sigmoid output.
Fine-tuning uses a small learning rate (5e-5) and updates the whole network; one epoch was enough here.
Fine-tuned RoBERTa base reaches 93.66% test accuracy on IMDb, beating chapter 14's 90% bigram ceiling; RoBERTa large would exceed 95%.
The accuracy gain comes with a large increase in inference cost compared with simple n-gram models.
Section 15.5 starts from Word2Vec: an embedding objective that turns word co-occurrence into vector (cosine) proximity.

questions.question: What does `x = x[:, 0, :]` do in Listing 15.22?
options: Keeps the first review of each batch
Keeps the hidden vector of the first token of each sequence
Averages the hidden vectors over all tokens
Keeps the first feature of every token vector
questions.answer: Keeps the hidden vector of the first token of each sequence
questions.explanation: The backbone output has shape (batch, sequence, 768). Indexing 0 on axis 1 selects the first token for every example, as the callout says. Axis 0 would be the batch (first review), averaging would be mean pooling, and indexing the last axis would pick a single feature.

questions.question: How many epochs does Listing 15.23 train for, and how can you tell?
questions.answer: One epoch: `fit()` is called without an `epochs` argument, and Keras defaults to 1; the text confirms 'In just a single epoch of training'.
questions.explanation: The default value of `epochs` in `Model.fit()` is 1, which matches the authors' statement.

questions.question: Why is the learning rate set to 5e-5 instead of Adam's default 1e-3 when fine-tuning RoBERTa?
questions.answer: The backbone's weights already encode valuable knowledge from pretraining; large updates (especially while the new head is still random and produces large, noisy gradients) could destroy it. A small learning rate adapts the representations gently.
questions.explanation: This is the essence of fine-tuning versus training from scratch; the book uses 5e-5 without discussing it, so the reasoning here is an explanation beyond the page.

questions.question: The test output is `[0.168127179145813, 0.9366399645805359]`. If the test set has 25,000 reviews, roughly how many were misclassified? And what geometric-mean probability of the correct label does a loss of 0.168 correspond to?
questions.explanation: Accuracy is the fraction correct, so errors = 25,000 × 0.06336. Binary cross-entropy averages $-\ln p_{\text{correct}}$, so exponentiating the negative mean loss gives the geometric mean of $p_{\text{correct}}$. (The 25,000 figure is the standard IMDb test size, an assumption here.)

questions.question: According to the page, what is the main downside of the RoBERTa classifier compared with chapter 14's bigram model?
options: It is far more expensive to use
It needs many epochs to converge
questions.answer: It is far more expensive to use
questions.explanation: The authors say 'this is a far more expensive model to use than the simple bigram classifier'. It used the same labeled data, the subword tokenizer handles any word (p.480), and it converged in one epoch.

questions.question: What was Word2Vec's training objective, as described at the start of section 15.5?
questions.answer: To turn correlation relationships between words into distance relationships: each word gets a vector, optimized so that vectors of frequently co-occurring words have a dot-product (cosine proximity) close to 1 and those of rarely co-occurring words close to 0.
questions.explanation: The first half of this is on this page; the 'close to 0' half finishes the sentence on p.486.

questions.question: Could you explain to a colleague why fine-tuned RoBERTa beats chapter 14's LSTM by about 10 points of accuracy on the same data?
questions.answer: Self-check: mention that the LSTM had to learn embeddings from 20,000 reviews and overfitted before learning good ones (p.437), while RoBERTa arrives with representations learned from 160 GB of text (p.479) and only needs to adapt them.
questions.explanation: If you can connect the result to the data-hunger argument of chapter 14, you understand why pretraining matters.
